extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, and researchers interested in the Volkswagen emissions scandal and automotive regulation
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic summary detailing the Volkswagen TDI/‘Dieselgate’ emissions scandal: its technical basis, regulatory responses, media coverage, public polling, and legal/enforcement outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of defeat devices under EU Regulation 715/2007 (Euro 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 5 (2) of Euro 6 Regulation 715/2007/EC prohibits the use of defeat devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page quotes the regulation and explains that the prohibition is legally binding for vehicles subject to Euro 6. This is the core regulatory standard used to judge whether Volkswagen’s software was illegal in the EU context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a 'defeat device' (Article 3(10) wording)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 3(10) defines defeat device as “any element of design which senses temperature, vehicle speed, engine speed (RPM), transmission gear, manifold vacuum or any other parameter for the purpose of activating, modulating, delaying or deactivating the operation of any part of the emission control system, that reduces the effectiveness of the emission control system under conditions which may reasonably be expected to be encountered in normal vehicle operation and use.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition establishes the evaluative criteria for whether particular software or hardware constitutes an illegal defeat device: it must (a) sense operational parameters and (b) change emission-control behavior in ways that reduce effectiveness under normal driving conditions. The article cites this language when explaining regulators’ findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory enforcement standard and remedies (EPA / CARB / KBA actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators (EPA, California CARB, Germany's KBA, etc.) may determine Clean Air Act/other violations, issue Notices of Violation, order recalls, and require removal of software and other remedial measures to ensure emissions rules are fulfilled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents examples: EPA/CARB notifications of Clean Air Act violations, U.S. orders to recall hundreds of thousands of cars, and KBA’s compulsory recall order requiring VW to remove the software and take measures to ensure compliance. It contrasts enforcement powers and typical remedies (recall, software/hardware fixes, compensation, civil/criminal fines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between voluntary and compulsory recalls (procedural/consumer-impact standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary recall: manufacturer offers repair and motorists decide whether to present vehicles for remedy. Compulsory recall (as ordered by authorities like KBA): mandates removal of prohibited software and obliges manufacturer to implement fixes for all affected vehicles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains the practical and legal difference — voluntary leaves onus on owners; compulsory recall legally forces remediation. It cites KBA ordering compulsory recall and VW’s initial proposal of a voluntary recall as an example of the difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable emissions testing standards and methods (lab FTP‑75 vs real‑world PEMS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lab test cycles (e.g., FTP‑75) have been the conventional standard for certification, but portable emissions measurement systems (PEMS) and on‑road testing reveal real‑world NOx emissions often exceed lab results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text references FTP‑75, JRC/ICCT studies, and PEMS testing (e.g., West Virginia University study and JRC reports) to show how testing methodology affects measured compliance. The implication is that robust evaluation of emissions requires on-road/PEMS methods in addition to lab cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustainability/index membership criteria (Dow Jones Sustainability index standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustainability indices (e.g., Dow Jones Sustainability indexes, RobecoSAM) evaluate companies on social and ethical grounds and may de-list companies for social/ethical failings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes RobecoSAM and S&P Dow Jones Indices stated Volkswagen would be de‑listed, citing social and ethical reasons and removal as an Industry Group Leader — illustrating that corporate sustainability rankings incorporate non‑technical ethical criteria and can be used as reputational/evaluative sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award criteria for 'Green Car of the Year' (environmental performance benchmark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Green Car Journal’s 'Green Car of the Year' recognizes models that 'best raise the bar in environmental performance'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page reports that Green Car Journal rescinded past awards to Volkswagen models, demonstrating that industry awards use explicit environmental-performance criteria and may be revoked if later evidence shows non‑compliance or deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and enforcement outcomes as evaluative measures (civil/criminal charges, fines, settlements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal outcomes — DOJ complaints, indictments, criminal fines, civil settlements, and court rulings — are used to measure the severity and legal validation of wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists many enforcement outcomes (DOJ complaint, $14.7bn U.S. settlement, criminal fines, indictments of executives, German fines and consumer settlements) as indicators of regulatory/legal judgment and the consequences companies face when found to have violated emissions and consumer‑protection laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputational impact metrics (public polling and market reactions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion polls (e.g., percent of consumers with positive/negative impressions, trust metrics) and market indicators (stock de‑valuations, de‑listings) are used to evaluate reputational damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites multiple polls (Bild, Prophet, Kellogg/Survata, AutoPacific) and market reactions (Volkswagen stock drops, media headlines) showing how public sentiment and financial markets quantify reputational harm after a scandal.
